final_proof:
Let
\[
w_k=e^{2\pi i k/n}\qquad (k=0,1,\ldots,n-1).
\]
These are precisely the elements of \(U_n\) (using any complete set of \(n\) consecutive integer representatives gives the same set). Indeed, \(w_k^n=e^{2\pi i k}=1\). Conversely, if \(z^n=1\), write \(z=re^{i\theta}\), where \(r>0\). Taking absolute values gives \(r^n=1\), hence \(r=1\); and \(e^{in\theta}=1\) gives \(n\theta=2\pi m\) for some \(m\in\mathbb Z\). Thus \(z=e^{2\pi i m/n}=w_k\), where \(k\) is the residue of \(m\) modulo \(n\). In particular, the particular number \(z\) in the hypothesis belongs to \(U_n\).

The points \(w_0,\ldots,w_{n-1}\) are distinct. For if \(w_j=w_k\), then \(e^{2\pi i(j-k)/n}=1\), so \(n\mid(j-k)\); since \(0\le j,k<n\), this forces \(j=k\). Also
\[
|w_k|=|e^{2\pi i k/n}|=1,
\]
so all these points lie on the unit circle \(C:|z|=1\), whose center is the origin. Their arguments \(0,2\pi/n,\ldots,2\pi(n-1)/n\) show that they occur around \(C\) in the cyclic order \(w_0,w_1,\ldots,w_{n-1}\). Joining consecutive points in this order, with \(w_n:=w_0\), therefore gives a convex \(n\)-gon \(P\). For completeness, no listed point can fail to be a vertex: the tangent line to \(C\) at \(w_k\) is a supporting line of the closed unit disk and meets \(C\) only at \(w_k\).

Put \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/n}\). Since \(w_{k+1}=\omega w_k\), for every \(k\), with indices read modulo \(n\),
\[
|w_{k+1}-w_k|=|w_k|\,|\omega-1|=|e^{2\pi i/n}-1|=\sqrt{2-2\cos(2\pi/n)}=2\sin(\pi/n).
\]
Thus all sides of \(P\) have the same length. Moreover, multiplication by \(\omega\) is rotation through \(2\pi/n\) about the origin, and it maps \(w_k\) to \(w_{k+1}\) and each side of \(P\) to the following side. Because a rotation preserves angles and maps the interior of this convex polygon to itself, it maps the interior angle at \(w_k\) to the interior angle at \(w_{k+1}\). Hence all interior angles are equal as well. Therefore \(P\) is a regular \(n\)-sided polygon.

Every vertex of \(P\) lies on \(C\), so \(C\) is the unit circle circumscribed about \(P\), and its center is \(0\), corresponding to \((0,0)\) in the complex plane. Finally,
\[
w_0=e^0=1,
\]
which corresponds to the point \((1,0)\). Thus both asserted properties hold.
